stem: You create a Deployment without setting `.spec.strategy`. How does Kubernetes replace Pods when you later change the container image?

options.text: A rolling update: new Pods start while old ones are removed in steps
options.why: RollingUpdate is the default strategy, with maxSurge and maxUnavailable both 25%.

options.text: It deletes every old Pod first, then creates all the new Pods at once
options.why: That is the Recreate strategy, which you have to set explicitly.

options.text: It keeps the old Pods running and waits for you to delete them
options.why: Deployments roll out automatically; manual replacement is the OnDelete strategy of StatefulSets and DaemonSets.

options.text: It creates a full second set of Pods and swaps traffic in one step
options.why: That is blue/green, which a single Deployment does not do; it needs two Deployments or a delivery tool.

explanation: A Deployment defaults to `strategy.type: RollingUpdate` with `maxSurge: 25%` and `maxUnavailable: 25%`. The controller creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods from the old one to the new one in steps, so the application keeps serving throughout.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Strategy)

stem: Running `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=8` creates a new Deployment revision that `kubectl rollout undo` can later return to.

options.text: True
options.why: Scaling changes `.spec.replicas`, not the Pod template, so no new revision or ReplicaSet is created.

options.text: False
options.why: Only changes to `.spec.template` create a revision; scaling just resizes the current ReplicaSet.

explanation: A new revision is created if and only if the Pod template (`.spec.template`) changes, for example the image or template labels. Scaling is deliberately excluded so that you can scale (manually or with an HPA) while a rollout or rollback is happening.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Checking rollout history)

stem: By default, how many old ReplicaSets does a Deployment keep so that you can roll back to them? (This is the default value of `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit`.) Type a number.
explanation: `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit` defaults to 10. Older ReplicaSets beyond that are garbage-collected. Setting it to 0 removes all history, so `kubectl rollout undo` then has nothing to roll back to.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Clean up policy)

stem: A Deployment uses `strategy: { type: Recreate }`. What happens when you update its image?

options.text: All old Pods are terminated before any new Pod is created, so there is a gap
options.why: Recreate kills the old ReplicaSet's Pods first, which means downtime between the two versions.

options.text: New Pods are created first, then the old ones are removed once they are ready
options.why: That surge-then-remove behaviour is RollingUpdate, not Recreate.

options.text: Kubernetes restarts the containers in place inside the existing Pods one by one
options.why: A Deployment never edits running Pods for an image change; it always creates new Pods.

options.text: Only Pods on nodes that already cached the new image are replaced immediately
options.why: Image caching affects pull time, not which Pods a strategy replaces.

explanation: With Recreate, all existing Pods are killed before new ones are created. It is useful when two versions must never run at the same time (for example an incompatible schema, or a single ReadWriteOnce volume), at the cost of a short outage.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Recreate Deployment)

stem: Match each autoscaler with what it changes.

options.text: The number of Pod replicas of a workload
The CPU and memory requests of a workload's Pods
The number of nodes in the cluster
Replica count driven by event sources such as queue length, including down to zero

explanation: HPA scales out (more replicas), VPA scales up (bigger requests per Pod), and the Cluster Autoscaler changes the number of nodes so Pods have somewhere to run. KEDA drives replica counts from external event sources and can scale a workload to zero, managing an HPA for the 1-to-N range.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Autoscaling Workloads

stem: An HPA targets `averageUtilization: 50` for CPU. One Pod requests `200m` CPU, has a `1` CPU limit, and is currently using `150m`. What CPU utilisation does the HPA see for this Pod?

options.text: 75%, because utilisation is measured against the 200m request
options.why: HPA resource utilisation is usage divided by the container requests: 150m / 200m = 75%.

options.text: 15%, because utilisation is measured against the 1-CPU limit
options.why: Limits play no part in the HPA utilisation calculation.

options.text: 50%, because the HPA reports the target as the current value
options.why: The HPA reports the measured value; the target is only what it compares against.

options.text: Unknown, because utilisation needs the limit and request to match
options.why: Requests and limits don't have to match; the HPA only needs requests to be set.

explanation: For `Resource` metrics with a utilisation target, the controller computes usage as a percentage of the containers' resource requests. Here 150m / 200m = 75%, which is above the 50% target, so this Pod pushes the average up and the HPA would scale out.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (How it works)

stem: Which changes to a Deployment start a new rollout, that is, a new ReplicaSet? (Choose two.)

options.text: Changing the container image in the Pod template
options.why: The image lives in `.spec.template`, so changing it creates a new revision.

options.text: Adding a label under `.spec.template.metadata.labels`
options.why: Template labels are part of the Pod template, so this also rolls out new Pods.

options.text: Changing `.spec.replicas` from 3 to 6
options.why: Scaling resizes the current ReplicaSet and creates no new revision.

options.text: Adding an annotation to the Deployment's own `.metadata`
options.why: The Deployment object's metadata is outside the Pod template.

options.text: Changing `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit`
options.why: This only controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept.

explanation: A rollout is triggered if and only if `.spec.template` changes. Images, environment variables, resources and template labels or annotations all live there. Replicas, history limits and the Deployment's own metadata do not.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Updating a Deployment)

stem: A PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 2` guarantees that at least 2 of its Pods keep running even if the nodes they are on crash.

options.text: True
options.why: PDBs can't prevent involuntary disruptions such as hardware failure or a kernel panic.

options.text: False
options.why: A PDB only limits voluntary disruptions that go through the Eviction API, such as `kubectl drain`.

explanation: PodDisruptionBudgets apply to voluntary disruptions: evictions requested through the Eviction API, used by node drains and the Cluster Autoscaler. Node crashes, OOM kills and direct deletes are involuntary and ignore PDBs, so you still need enough replicas spread across failure domains.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Disruptions

stem: A Deployment has `replicas: 10` and the default rolling update settings (25% surge, 25% unavailable). During a rollout, what is the maximum total number of Pods, and the minimum number that must stay available?

options.text: At most 13 Pods in total, with at least 8 available
options.why: maxSurge 25% of 10 = 2.5, rounded up to 3; maxUnavailable 2.5 rounded down to 2.

options.text: At most 12 Pods in total, with at least 8 available
options.why: This rounds the surge down; maxSurge percentages are rounded up.

options.text: At most 13 Pods in total, with at least 7 available
options.why: This rounds maxUnavailable up; it is rounded down, so 2 may be unavailable.

options.text: At most 12 Pods in total, with at least 7 available
options.why: Both roundings are reversed here.

explanation: Percentages are converted to Pod counts with maxSurge rounded up and maxUnavailable rounded down: surge = ceil(2.5) = 3, so up to 10 + 3 = 13 Pods; unavailable = floor(2.5) = 2, so at least 10 − 2 = 8 must be available. The asymmetry errs on the side of availability.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Max Surge, Max Unavailable)

stem: An HPA targets 60% average CPU utilisation. The Deployment runs 4 Pods averaging 90% of their CPU requests. How many replicas does the HPA want? Type a number.
explanation: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric) = ceil(4 × 90 / 60) = ceil(6.0) = 6. The ratio 1.5 is far outside the default 0.1 tolerance, so the HPA acts.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Algorithm details)

stem: You run `app-blue` and `app-green` Deployments, labelled `version: blue` and `version: green`, behind one Service whose selector is `app: shop, version: blue`. How do you cut all traffic over to green in one step?

options.text: Change the Service selector to `version: green`
options.why: The Service immediately selects only green Pods, and switching back is just as quick.

options.text: Scale `app-blue` to zero and let the Service find green
options.why: The selector still says blue, so the Service would end up with no endpoints at all.

options.text: Run `kubectl rollout undo` on `app-blue` to reach green
options.why: Undo moves blue to its own previous template; it knows nothing about the green Deployment.

options.text: Add a `version: green` label to the Service's metadata
options.why: Labels on the Service object don't affect which Pods it selects.

explanation: Blue/green on plain Kubernetes means running both versions in full and flipping the Service selector (or an Ingress/Gateway backend) from one to the other. The cutover is atomic from the Service's point of view, rollback is the same flip in reverse, and the price is running double capacity during the switch.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Service (selectors); Deployments

stem: A Deployment with `replicas: 3`, `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0` gets a new image. Put the first steps of the rollout in order.

options.text: The new ReplicaSet is scaled up by one Pod
That new Pod passes readiness and counts as available
The old ReplicaSet is scaled down by one Pod
The new ReplicaSet is scaled up by another Pod

explanation: With maxSurge 1 the controller may run 4 Pods, so it first adds one new Pod. With maxUnavailable 0 it can't remove an old Pod until that new Pod is available (Ready for minReadySeconds). Only then does it scale the old ReplicaSet down to 2 and add the next new Pod, repeating until all 3 are new.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Rolling Update Deployment)

stem: A rollout has been stuck for 10 minutes because the new Pods never pass their readiness probe. The Deployment uses the default `progressDeadlineSeconds`. What does Kubernetes do?

options.text: Sets Progressing=False (ProgressDeadlineExceeded) but takes no other action
options.why: The condition is a signal for you or your tooling; the controller doesn't revert anything.

options.text: Rolls back to the previous ReplicaSet automatically and records a new revision
options.why: Deployments never roll back on their own; you run `kubectl rollout undo` or a tool does.

options.text: Deletes the new ReplicaSet and pauses the Deployment until you resume it
options.why: The new ReplicaSet stays, and the Deployment isn't paused.

options.text: Restarts the rollout from the beginning with the progress deadline doubled
options.why: There is no automatic retry or deadline extension.

explanation: `progressDeadlineSeconds` defaults to 600. When it passes without progress, the Deployment controller adds a `Progressing` condition with `status: False` and `reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. `kubectl rollout status` then exits non-zero, which CI can use to trigger a rollback, but the controller itself takes no further action.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Failed Deployment)

stem: `kubectl get hpa` shows `<unknown>/70%` for a CPU-utilisation HPA, and it never scales. Which two causes are plausible? (Choose two.)

options.text: metrics-server isn't installed or isn't serving metrics.k8s.io
options.why: Resource metrics come from the metrics API, which metrics-server usually provides.

options.text: A container in the target Pods has no CPU request set
options.why: Utilisation is a percentage of requests, so a missing request makes it undefined.

options.text: maxReplicas is lower than the current number of replicas
options.why: That caps the result but doesn't make the current metric unknown.

options.text: The Deployment uses Recreate rather than RollingUpdate
options.why: The rollout strategy has no effect on how metrics are read.

options.text: The Pods have a liveness probe but no readiness probe
options.why: Probes affect readiness handling, not whether a CPU metric exists.

explanation: An `<unknown>` current value means the HPA can't compute the metric. The usual causes are that the resource metrics API (metrics-server) isn't available, or that some container in the Pods lacks a CPU request, which leaves utilisation undefined. `kubectl describe hpa` shows events such as `FailedGetResourceMetric`.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling

stem: Behind one Service you run 9 Pods of v1 and 1 Pod of v2, all matching the Service selector. Roughly what share of requests reaches v2, and what is the limitation of this canary?

options.text: About 10%, but the split tracks Pod counts, so 1% needs about 99 v1 Pods
options.why: The Service spreads connections across endpoints, so the ratio follows the number of Pods.

options.text: Exactly 10%, because kube-proxy enforces a strict per-request round robin
options.why: kube-proxy balances connections (randomly in iptables mode), so the split is only approximate.

options.text: About 50%, because kube-proxy balances per ReplicaSet and not per Pod
options.why: kube-proxy only sees endpoints; it has no idea which ReplicaSet a Pod belongs to.

options.text: None at first, because a Service routes only to the newest ReplicaSet
options.why: Any Ready Pod matching the selector receives traffic, old or new.

explanation: A replica-ratio canary is easy but coarse: traffic follows Pod counts and is spread per connection, not per request. Fine-grained splits such as 1% or 5%, or routing by header, need traffic management from Gateway API HTTPRoute weights, a service mesh, or a tool like Argo Rollouts or Flagger.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Managing Resources (Canary deployments)

stem: Revisions 1, 2 and 3 of a Deployment exist and revision 3 is live. You run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` with no other flags. What happens?

options.text: The Pod template of revision 2 is rolled out again
options.why: Without `--to-revision`, undo goes to the previous revision.

options.text: The Deployment goes back to revision 1, the original
options.why: Only `--to-revision=1` would select the first revision.

options.text: Revision 3 is deleted and the running Pods stay as they are
options.why: Undo performs a normal rollout to the older template.

options.text: The command fails because `--to-revision` is required
options.why: The flag is optional; the default is the previous revision.

explanation: `kubectl rollout undo` rolls the Deployment back to the previous revision by re-applying that ReplicaSet's Pod template through a normal rolling update. Use `kubectl rollout history` to see revisions and `--to-revision=N` to pick a specific one.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Rolling Back a Deployment)

stem: With the default feature gates in Kubernetes 1.33, you can set `minReplicas: 0` on an HPA that scales on CPU utilisation, and it will scale the Deployment to zero when idle.

options.text: True
options.why: Scale-to-zero needs the HPAScaleToZero feature gate, which is alpha and off by default.

options.text: False
options.why: It needs a non-default feature gate, and even then only for object or external metrics.

explanation: The HPAScaleToZero feature gate is alpha (disabled by default) and only allows `minReplicas: 0` for object and external metrics, not CPU utilisation: with zero Pods there is nothing to measure. Event-driven tools such as KEDA are the usual way to scale to and from zero.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Scaling to and from zero)

stem: A Deployment sets `minReadySeconds: 30`. What does this change during a rolling update?

options.text: A new Pod counts as available only after being Ready for 30 seconds
options.why: The rollout only moves on once new Pods have stayed Ready that long, which catches early crashes.

options.text: The controller waits 30 seconds before it creates any new Pods at all
options.why: Creation starts immediately; the delay applies to counting Pods as available.

options.text: Each container gets 30 seconds before its liveness probe starts running
options.why: Probe timing is set with probe fields such as `initialDelaySeconds` or a startup probe.

options.text: Old Pods get 30 extra seconds of grace period before they are killed
options.why: The termination grace period is `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, a Pod spec field.

explanation: `minReadySeconds` (default 0) is the minimum time a newly created Pod must be Ready, with no container crashing, before it is considered available. Because maxUnavailable and progress are measured in available Pods, it slows the rollout so a Pod that passes readiness and then crashes doesn't let the rollout race ahead.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Min Ready Seconds)

stem: Which two statements correctly contrast Karpenter with the Cluster Autoscaler? (Choose two.)

options.text: Cluster Autoscaler resizes predefined node groups, such as cloud autoscaling groups
options.why: It works through node groups you set up in advance, each with a fixed instance shape.

options.text: Karpenter chooses instance types for pending Pods directly, without fixed node groups
options.why: It provisions nodes that fit the pending Pods' requirements and consolidates them later.

options.text: Karpenter scales Pods horizontally, while Cluster Autoscaler scales Pods vertically
options.why: Both scale nodes; neither changes Pod replicas or Pod requests.

options.text: Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when average node CPU usage rises above a threshold
options.why: It reacts to Pods that can't be scheduled, not to node CPU usage.

options.text: Karpenter only works for Pods that have no resource requests set at all
options.why: Karpenter relies on requests to size nodes, just like the scheduler.

explanation: Both are node autoscalers driven by unschedulable Pods. Cluster Autoscaler grows and shrinks node groups you defined in advance. Karpenter provisions nodes on demand, picking instance types that fit the pending Pods' requirements, and consolidates underused nodes, which usually gives faster and better-fitted scaling.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Node Autoscaling

stem: A Deployment sets both `maxSurge: 0` and `maxUnavailable: 0` in its rolling update strategy. What happens when you apply it?

options.text: The API server rejects it, since both values can't be zero at once
options.why: Validation forbids it: with no surge and no unavailability the rollout could never make progress.

options.text: Rollouts replace one Pod at a time, never adding or removing extras
options.why: Replacing a Pod needs either an extra Pod (surge) or a missing one (unavailable).

options.text: The Deployment is accepted, but every rollout stalls until its deadline
options.why: It never gets that far; the object fails validation.

options.text: Kubernetes quietly replaces both values with the 25% defaults
options.why: Explicit values are validated, not swapped for defaults.

explanation: The Deployment documentation states that maxUnavailable can't be 0 if maxSurge is 0, and API validation rejects the combination. To roll one Pod at a time with no capacity loss, use `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0`. To avoid extra Pods, use `maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1`.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Max Unavailable)

stem: A Deployment has `replicas: 3`, `maxSurge: 50%` and `maxUnavailable: 50%`. During a rollout, what are the maximum total Pods and the minimum available Pods?

options.text: At most 5 Pods, with at least 2 available
options.why: Surge: ceil(1.5) = 2, so 3 + 2 = 5. Unavailable: floor(1.5) = 1, so 3 − 1 = 2.

options.text: At most 4 Pods, with at least 1 available
options.why: Both roundings are reversed here.

options.text: At most 5 Pods, with at least 1 available
options.why: maxUnavailable is rounded down, so only 1 Pod may be unavailable.

options.text: At most 4 Pods, with at least 2 available
options.why: maxSurge is rounded up, so 2 extra Pods are allowed.

explanation: For small replica counts the rounding rule matters a lot: 50% of 3 is 1.5. maxSurge rounds up to 2 (up to 5 Pods in total) and maxUnavailable rounds down to 1 (at least 2 available). Rounding is biased toward keeping capacity.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Max Surge, Max Unavailable)

stem: An HPA targets 60% CPU utilisation. The Deployment has 10 replicas averaging 65%. With the default tolerance, what does the HPA do?

options.text: Nothing: 65/60 ≈ 1.08 is inside the 0.1 tolerance
options.why: Ratios between 0.9 and 1.1 are treated as close enough to the target.

options.text: Scales to 11, since ceil(10 × 65 ÷ 60) gives 11 Pods
options.why: The formula would give 11, but the tolerance check comes first and skips the change.

options.text: Scales to 12, because it always adds a 20% buffer
options.why: There is no built-in buffer; the result comes straight from the formula.

options.text: Scales down to 9, because it is within 10% of target
options.why: Being within tolerance means no change at all, in either direction.

explanation: The controller computes ratio = currentMetric / target = 65 / 60 ≈ 1.083. Because |1.083 − 1| < 0.1 (the default tolerance), it skips scaling and stays at 10, which prevents flapping on small fluctuations. Outside the tolerance it would use ceil(10 × 1.083) = 11.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Algorithm details)

stem: An HPA has two metrics. CPU alone would ask for 5 replicas, and a requests-per-second metric alone would ask for 8. The current count is 4 and `maxReplicas` is 10. How many replicas does it set?

options.text: 8, the largest of the per-metric proposals
options.why: With several metrics the HPA computes each proposal and takes the maximum.

options.text: 5, the smallest proposal, to save capacity
options.why: Taking the minimum would under-provision for the busier metric.

options.text: 7, the rounded average of the two proposals
options.why: Proposals are never averaged.

options.text: 10, since conflicting metrics mean max
options.why: Disagreement doesn't push the HPA to maxReplicas.

explanation: When an HPA has multiple metrics, it calculates a desired replica count for each and uses the largest, so the workload is sized for whichever signal needs the most capacity. The result is still clamped to minReplicas and maxReplicas.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Scaling on multiple metrics)

stem: Argo CD syncs a Deployment manifest that contains `replicas: 3`. An HPA on the same Deployment scales it to 9 under load, but the count keeps snapping back to 3. What is the right fix?

options.text: Remove `replicas` from the manifest so only the HPA owns it
options.why: Every sync re-applies `replicas: 3` and overwrites the HPA; leaving the field out ends the fight.

options.text: Raise the HPA's `minReplicas` to 9 so that both values always agree
options.why: That pins the Deployment at 9 and defeats autoscaling.

options.text: Delete the HPA and hard-code 9 replicas in the manifest
options.why: That gives up autoscaling instead of fixing the conflict.

options.text: Set `maxSurge: 6` so the rollout has room for 9 Pods
options.why: maxSurge only affects rollouts, not the steady replica count.

explanation: When an HPA manages a workload, the documentation recommends removing `spec.replicas` from the manifests. Otherwise every apply or GitOps sync resets the replica count, the HPA scales back up, and the two keep fighting. Argo CD can alternatively be told to ignore that field.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Migrating Deployments to horizontal autoscaling)

stem: Traffic drops sharply at 12:00, and a CPU-based HPA with default `behavior` immediately computes that 3 replicas are enough (down from 12). When does it reach 3?

options.text: Around 12:05: scale-down uses the highest target from the last 5 minutes
options.why: The default 300-second scale-down window holds the count until the higher recommendations age out.

options.text: Immediately, because scale-down policies allow removing 100% of Pods in 15s
options.why: The policy would allow it, but the stabilization window is applied first.

options.text: After about 15 minutes, because it removes only one Pod per minute by default
options.why: No one-Pod-per-minute default exists.

options.text: Never automatically, because scale-down always needs a manual kubectl scale
options.why: HPAs scale down on their own; they just do it cautiously.

explanation: By default `scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` is 300. The HPA uses the highest desired-replica recommendation from the past 5 minutes, which acts as a rolling maximum, so a brief dip doesn't remove capacity that is needed again moments later. Once the high recommendations age out (around 12:05), it can drop to 3.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Stabilization window)

stem: A Deployment with 10 replicas (default 25% surge and unavailable) is updated to an image that crashes on start. Which statement best describes the state a few minutes later?

options.text: At least 8 old Pods keep serving; the rollout stalls and is not reverted
options.why: maxUnavailable 2 lets the old ReplicaSet shrink to 8, and the controller can't remove more while new Pods are unavailable.

options.text: All 10 old Pods are gone, and the Service is left with no endpoints at all
options.why: The rolling update never drops below 10 − 2 = 8 available Pods.

options.text: The controller notices the crashes and rolls back to the old image
options.why: Deployments never roll back on their own.

options.text: Only 3 surge Pods crash, and all 10 old Pods stay untouched and Ready
options.why: The controller may scale the old ReplicaSet down to 8 within the unavailable budget.

explanation: The controller keeps total Pods ≤ 13 and available Pods ≥ 8. It can shrink the old ReplicaSet to 8 and fill the rest of the 13 with new Pods, but because those never become available it can't go further. Traffic is served by the 8 old Pods, and after `progressDeadlineSeconds` the Deployment reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Recovering means `kubectl rollout undo` or fixing the image.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Rolling Update, Failed Deployment)

stem: A Deployment of 4 replicas has a PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 3`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A `kubectl drain` evicts at most one of these Pods at a time
options.why: Drain uses the Eviction API, which refuses evictions that would leave fewer than 3 available.

options.text: A rolling update of the Deployment isn't limited by this PDB
options.why: The Deployment controller deletes Pods directly; its pace comes from maxUnavailable.

options.text: If two nodes crash at once, the PDB keeps 3 Pods running
options.why: Crashes are involuntary disruptions, which PDBs can't prevent.

options.text: The HPA can't scale this Deployment below 3 because of it
options.why: HPA scale-down changes replicas and doesn't go through the Eviction API.

options.text: Running `kubectl delete pod` on one of them is refused
options.why: Direct deletes bypass PDBs; only evictions are checked.

explanation: PDBs are enforced only by the Eviction API, which `kubectl drain` and the Cluster Autoscaler use. With 4 healthy Pods and minAvailable 3, only one eviction is allowed at a time. Rollouts, HPA scale-down, direct deletes and node failures don't go through eviction, so the PDB doesn't limit them.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Disruptions; Specifying a Disruption Budget

stem: During rollouts, clients see a few connection errors even though every Pod handles SIGTERM gracefully. Adding a `preStop` hook that sleeps 5–10 seconds fixes it. Why?

options.text: Endpoint removal propagates asynchronously, so requests still arrive after SIGTERM
options.why: kube-proxy, ingress controllers and load balancers learn about the removal with a delay, and the sleep covers that gap.

options.text: The sleep gives the new Pod's readiness probe time to pass before the old ones stop
options.why: Old Pods are only removed once new ones are available, so readiness isn't the issue.

options.text: preStop hooks add the sleep time to terminationGracePeriodSeconds on top of it
options.why: The preStop hook runs inside the grace period; it doesn't extend it.

options.text: Kubernetes waits for preStop to finish before it creates any replacement Pods
options.why: Replacements are created independently of the old Pod's shutdown.

explanation: When a Pod starts terminating, removal from the EndpointSlices and the SIGTERM delivery happen in parallel. Proxies and external load balancers may keep routing to the Pod for a few seconds, so an app that exits immediately drops those requests. A short preStop sleep keeps it serving until routing catches up, and the sleep must fit inside `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Pod Lifecycle (Termination of Pods); Container Lifecycle Hooks

stem: Put the steps of a blue/green cutover with two Deployments and one Service in order.

options.text: Deploy green alongside blue and wait until all its Pods are Ready
Smoke-test green through a separate test Service or port-forward
Switch the main Service selector from blue to green
Keep blue running for a while so you can switch back quickly
Delete the blue Deployment once green has proved itself

explanation: Blue/green brings the new version up in full, tests it without production traffic, then flips the selector in one step. Keeping blue around afterwards makes rollback another instant flip, and removing it later reclaims the double capacity.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Service; Deployments

stem: A Deployment has `replicas: 15`, `maxSurge: 10%` and `maxUnavailable: 10%`. What is the minimum number of Pods that must stay available during a rollout? Type a number.
explanation: 10% of 15 is 1.5. maxUnavailable is rounded down to 1, so at least 15 − 1 = 14 Pods must stay available. (maxSurge is rounded up to 2, allowing up to 17 Pods in total.)
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Max Unavailable)

stem: Nodes in a node group sit at 90% CPU usage, but every Pod is scheduled and none are Pending. What does the Cluster Autoscaler do?

options.text: Nothing: it only adds nodes when Pods can't be scheduled for lack of resources
options.why: Scale-up is triggered by unschedulable Pods, not by how busy the nodes are.

options.text: Adds a node, because it scales out whenever node CPU usage goes past 80%
options.why: Cluster Autoscaler has no usage-based scale-up threshold.

options.text: Adds a node and then tells the HPA to place its new Pods on that node right away
options.why: Cluster Autoscaler doesn't talk to the HPA or place Pods.

options.text: Evicts the busiest Pods so that the scheduler can spread them more evenly
options.why: Rebalancing running Pods is a descheduler job, not the autoscaler's.

explanation: The Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when Pods are Pending because no node has room for their requests. Busy but sufficient nodes are a Pod-level concern: an HPA adds replicas, and only if those replicas can't fit does the Cluster Autoscaler add capacity. This is why accurate requests matter.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Node Autoscaling; Cluster Autoscaler FAQ

stem: Match each VerticalPodAutoscaler `updateMode` with its behaviour.

options.text: Only computes recommendations and never changes Pods
Sets requests when a Pod is created and never changes them afterwards
Sets requests at creation and evicts running Pods to apply new values
Tries an in-place resize first and evicts only if that fails

explanation: The VPA recommender always computes recommendations. The update mode decides how they are applied: `Off` only reports them, `Initial` applies them at Pod creation, `Recreate` (the default) also evicts running Pods while respecting PDBs, and `InPlaceOrRecreate` uses in-place Pod resize, falling back to eviction. The old `Auto` mode is deprecated in favour of these explicit modes.
reference: Kubernetes autoscaler docs: Vertical Pod Autoscaler quick start

stem: A team enables a VPA in `Recreate` mode and a CPU-utilisation HPA on the same Deployment. What is the problem?

options.text: They fight: raised requests lower utilisation, so the HPA scales in
options.why: Both controllers act on the same CPU signal in opposite directions.

options.text: The API rejects a VPA and an HPA that both point at one Deployment
options.why: Nothing stops you creating both; the conflict shows up at runtime.

options.text: The HPA blocks VPA evictions, so its recommendations are never applied
options.why: The HPA has no say over evictions.

options.text: VPA only works with StatefulSets, so it ignores the Deployment entirely
options.why: VPA supports Deployments and other controllers.

explanation: HPA utilisation is usage divided by requests. When VPA raises the requests, utilisation drops and the HPA removes replicas; fewer replicas raise per-Pod usage, and the two loop. Don't combine them on the same CPU or memory metrics: use the HPA on custom or external metrics, or run VPA in `Off` mode for recommendations only.
reference: Kubernetes autoscaler docs: VPA known limitations

stem: Revisions 1, 2 and 3 exist and revision 3 is live. You run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=1`. What does `kubectl rollout history deployment/web` list afterwards?

options.text: Revisions 2, 3 and 4, where 4 holds revision 1's template
options.why: Rolling back re-uses revision 1's ReplicaSet and gives it the next revision number.

options.text: Revisions 1, 2 and 3, with revision 1 now marked as the current one
options.why: Revision numbers only increase; the rolled-back template gets a new number.

options.text: Revisions 1, 2, 3 and 4, where 4 duplicates revision 1
options.why: The old ReplicaSet is reused, so revision 1 no longer appears separately.

options.text: Only revision 1, since undo discards the newer history
options.why: Revisions 2 and 3 remain available for further rollbacks.

explanation: A rollback is a rollout to an older template. The Deployment controller reuses the matching ReplicaSet and assigns it the next revision number, so revision 1 becomes revision 4 and disappears from the list under its old number. Revisions 2 and 3 are still there.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Rolling Back to a Previous Revision)

stem: A queue consumer uses KEDA with `minReplicaCount: 0`. How does scaling work between 0, 1 and N replicas?

options.text: KEDA itself activates 0↔1, and the HPA that it manages scales 1↔N
options.why: KEDA creates and owns an HPA for the 1-to-N range, and handles waking from zero itself.

options.text: KEDA replaces the HPA entirely and sets every replica count from 0 to N
options.why: KEDA deliberately builds on the HPA rather than replacing it.

options.text: The HPA scales 0↔N, because KEDA turns on HPAScaleToZero cluster-wide
options.why: KEDA doesn't change feature gates; it implements activation on its own.

options.text: KEDA only does scale-to-zero, so you also write a separate HPA for 1↔N
options.why: The ScaledObject creates the HPA for you; adding another one would conflict.

explanation: A KEDA ScaledObject has two phases. In activation (0 ↔ 1) the KEDA operator itself scales the workload when the event source becomes active or idle. In scaling (1 ↔ N) KEDA exposes the event metric through the external metrics API to an HPA it creates and manages. That lets queue consumers cost nothing while idle.
reference: KEDA docs: Scaling Deployments, StatefulSets and Custom Resources

stem: An HPA targets 70% CPU utilisation (a `Resource` metric). The app container requests 500m CPU, but an injected sidecar container in the same Pod has no CPU request. What happens?

options.text: The HPA can't compute Pod CPU utilisation and takes no action on that metric
options.why: Pod utilisation needs requests on every container; one missing request leaves it undefined.

options.text: The HPA ignores the sidecar and divides usage by the app container's request
options.why: A `Resource` metric covers the whole Pod; per-container targeting needs `ContainerResource`.

options.text: The HPA treats the sidecar as requesting 0m, so utilisation becomes infinite
options.why: It doesn't substitute zero; the utilisation is simply undefined.

options.text: The HPA falls back to using the sidecar's CPU limit as if it were the request
options.why: Limits are never used in place of requests for HPA utilisation.

explanation: The HPA documentation says that if some of a Pod's containers lack the relevant resource request, the Pod's utilisation is undefined and the autoscaler takes no action for that metric. Fix it by giving the sidecar a request (or a LimitRange default), or use a `ContainerResource` metric that targets only the app container.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Container resource metrics)

stem: An HPA with the default `behavior` runs 10 replicas. A spike makes it compute 40 desired replicas. Ignoring maxReplicas, how many replicas can it reach after the first 15-second period?

options.text: 20, since scale-up allows the larger of +100% or +4 Pods per 15s
options.why: Default scale-up policies are 100% and 4 Pods per 15 s with `selectPolicy: Max`, so +10.

options.text: 14, since the default scale-up adds at most 4 Pods every 15 seconds
options.why: With `selectPolicy: Max` the larger 100% policy wins over the 4-Pod one.

options.text: 40, since scale-up has no stabilization window and jumps straight there
options.why: There is no scale-up window, but the rate policies still cap each period.

options.text: 11, since scale-up is limited to a single Pod per period by default
options.why: No single-Pod default exists.

explanation: The default `scaleUp` behaviour has a stabilization window of 0 and two policies, 100% per 15 s and 4 Pods per 15 s, with `selectPolicy: Max`. At 10 replicas, 100% means +10, which beats +4, so the HPA can go to 20 in the first period and then to 40 after another.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Default behavior)

stem:
An HPA has 50 replicas and this scale-down behaviour:

```yaml
behavior:
  scaleDown:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
    selectPolicy: Min
    policies:
    - type: Pods
      value: 2
      periodSeconds: 60
    - type: Percent
      value: 10
      periodSeconds: 60
```

Load collapses. How many Pods can it remove in the first minute?

options.text: 2, because `Min` picks the policy allowing the smallest change
options.why: The Pods policy allows 2 and the Percent policy allows 5; Min selects 2.

options.text: 5, because 10% of 50 is bigger than the 2-Pod policy
options.why: That would be the result with the default `selectPolicy: Max`.

options.text: 7, because the limits of both policies are added together each minute
options.why: Policies are compared, not summed.

options.text: 45, because a zero window means nothing slows scale-down
options.why: The window is zero, but the rate policies still apply.

explanation: Each policy gives a maximum change per period: Pods allows 2, Percent allows 10% × 50 = 5. `selectPolicy: Max` (the default) uses the largest allowed change and `Min` the smallest, so here at most 2 Pods are removed per minute. `Disabled` would turn scale-down off.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Scaling policies)

stem: The Cluster Autoscaler reports a node as underutilised but never removes it. Which three could be the reason? (Choose three.)

options.text: A Pod on it has the annotation `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"`
options.why: This annotation explicitly tells the autoscaler not to evict that Pod.

options.text: A Pod on it isn't managed by any controller, so nothing would recreate it
options.why: Bare Pods block scale-down because evicting them would lose them for good.

options.text: Evicting its Pods would violate a PodDisruptionBudget
options.why: Cluster Autoscaler uses the Eviction API and respects PDBs.

options.text: It runs a DaemonSet Pod, such as a log collector or CNI agent
options.why: DaemonSet Pods don't block scale-down; they exist on every node anyway.

options.text: Its Pods mount a ConfigMap as a volume
options.why: ConfigMap volumes are recreated with the Pod elsewhere and don't block removal.

options.text: Its Pods have readiness probes configured
options.why: Probes have nothing to do with whether a node can be drained.

explanation: Before removing a node, the Cluster Autoscaler checks that every Pod on it can be moved. It is blocked by Pods with `safe-to-evict: "false"`, Pods without a controller, Pods whose eviction would breach a PDB, and (by default) non-DaemonSet kube-system Pods without a PDB. DaemonSet and mirror Pods are ignored.
reference: Kubernetes autoscaler docs: Cluster Autoscaler FAQ (What types of pods can prevent CA from removing a node?)

stem: To absorb sudden spikes without waiting minutes for new nodes, a team runs low-priority placeholder Pods (pause containers with a negative-priority PriorityClass) on spare capacity. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Real Pods preempt the placeholders, so they schedule at once on existing capacity
options.why: The scheduler evicts lower-priority Pods to make room for higher-priority ones.

options.text: The evicted placeholders go Pending, which makes the Cluster Autoscaler add a node
options.why: Pending placeholders trigger a scale-up in the background, rebuilding the buffer.

options.text: The placeholders make the HPA react faster by adding CPU load to the cluster
options.why: Pause containers use almost no CPU and have no effect on any HPA.

options.text: Placeholder Pods need the highest PriorityClass so that they are never evicted
options.why: They must have the lowest priority; their whole job is to be evicted.

options.text: This only works with Karpenter, since Cluster Autoscaler ignores Pod priority
options.why: This overprovisioning pattern is documented for Cluster Autoscaler.

explanation: Overprovisioning reserves headroom with Pods that request capacity but do nothing. Real workloads preempt them and start immediately, and the displaced placeholders become Pending, so the node autoscaler adds a node in the background to rebuild the buffer. It trades steady extra cost for removing node provisioning time from the critical path.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Overprovision Node Capacity for a Cluster

stem: You run `kubectl rollout pause deployment/web`, then change the image, an environment variable and a resource limit in three separate `kubectl apply` calls, then run `kubectl rollout resume deployment/web`. How many new rollouts start?

options.text: One rollout, carrying all three changes in a single new ReplicaSet
options.why: While paused, template changes pile up; resuming rolls them out together.

options.text: Three rollouts, one queued up for each separate change made during the pause
options.why: Pausing doesn't queue rollouts; it batches the changes into one.

options.text: None until you also run `kubectl rollout restart` on it
options.why: Resume alone starts the rollout of the accumulated changes.

options.text: Two: one for the image and one for the env and limit together
options.why: All template changes made while paused are combined.

explanation: Pausing a Deployment stops the controller from acting on Pod template changes. You can apply several fixes, and when you resume, a single rollout delivers the combined template. That avoids several back-to-back rollouts and the revisions they would leave behind.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Deployments (Pausing and Resuming a rollout)

stem: A CPU-based HPA has just scaled from 4 to 6 Pods. While the 2 new Pods are still starting (not yet Ready, no metrics), the HPA recalculates. How does it treat those 2 Pods when deciding whether to scale up further?

options.text: As using 0% of the target, which damps further scale-up
options.why: This conservative assumption keeps startup Pods from triggering runaway scale-ups.

options.text: As using 100% of the target, which speeds up any further scale-up
options.why: The 100% assumption applies to missing metrics on scale-down, not scale-up.

options.text: As copies of the ready Pods' average utilisation
options.why: The HPA never invents metrics by copying other Pods.

options.text: It ignores them and divides only by the 4 ready Pods
options.why: They are set aside at first, then counted with a conservative value.

explanation: The HPA sets aside Pods that are not yet Ready or have no metrics. If the remaining Pods suggest scaling up, it recalculates assuming those Pods use 0% of the desired value (and 100% for missing metrics when scaling down). If that dampened result reverses the direction or falls within tolerance, it skips scaling. This stops a scale-up from snowballing while new Pods warm up.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Algorithm details)

stem: Compared with a plain Deployment, which three capabilities do progressive-delivery setups (Argo Rollouts or Flagger, with a service mesh or Gateway API) add for canary releases? (Choose three.)

options.text: Weighted traffic splits such as 5% that don't depend on Pod counts
options.why: The router sends a set share of requests to the canary, however many Pods it has.

options.text: Automated metric analysis that promotes or aborts each canary step
options.why: Tools query metrics such as error rate or latency between steps.

options.text: Automatic rollback when the canary analysis fails
options.why: A failed analysis shifts traffic back to stable without manual action.

options.text: Readiness gating, so new Pods only get traffic once they are Ready
options.why: Plain Deployments and Services already gate traffic on readiness.

options.text: Keeping old ReplicaSets so that `kubectl rollout undo` works
options.why: Revision history is built into every Deployment.

options.text: Running two versions side by side during a release
options.why: A plain rolling update already runs old and new Pods together.

explanation: A plain Deployment gives readiness-gated rolling updates and manual undo. Progressive-delivery tools add traffic weights decoupled from replica counts (via mesh or Gateway API routing), metric-driven analysis at each step, and automatic promotion or rollback, which turns a canary from a manual process into a guarded pipeline.
reference: Kubernetes Gateway API docs: Traffic splitting; Argo Rollouts docs: Canary

stem: By default, an HPA applies a stabilization window to scale-down decisions but not to scale-up decisions.

options.text: True
options.why: Defaults are 300 seconds for scale-down and 0 seconds for scale-up.

options.text: False
options.why: Scale-up has a default window of 0, so it reacts immediately within its rate policies.

explanation: The default behaviour is asymmetric on purpose: react fast to rising load (`scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0`) and slowly to falling load (`scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300`). Both can be tuned per HPA through `spec.behavior`.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (Default behavior)

stem: What does `kubectl rollout restart deployment/web` actually do?

options.text: Patches a `restartedAt` annotation into the Pod template, so a normal rollout runs
options.why: Changing the template creates a new ReplicaSet that follows the usual strategy.

options.text: Restarts the containers in place inside the existing Pods, and creates no new ReplicaSet
options.why: Kubernetes has no in-place restart for Deployments; new Pods are created.

options.text: Deletes all the Pods at once so that the ReplicaSet recreates them immediately
options.why: That would cause downtime; restart respects maxSurge and maxUnavailable.

options.text: Rolls back to the previous revision and then forward again to the current one
options.why: No rollback happens; a new revision with the same spec plus an annotation is created.

explanation: `kubectl rollout restart` sets the annotation `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` in `.spec.template.metadata.annotations`. Because the template changed, the Deployment controller performs a regular rolling update, creating fresh Pods (for example to pick up a changed Secret) without downtime.
reference: Kubernetes docs: kubectl rollout restart
